sections.markdown:
## C — Safe and responsible driving part two: distraction and cell phone rules, road rage, drowsy driving, health and hearing, alcohol and drug impairment, implied consent and open containers, riding outside the vehicle, blowouts and brake failure
Knowledge domain: the conditions that make a driver unsafe, the Oregon device and sound rules, handling aggressive drivers and fatigue, how health and hearing matter, DUII, blood alcohol limits, implied consent and open container law, who may ride outside the cab, and what to do for blowouts and failed brakes; other equipment failures and fuel saving continue in part C2.

FACT_ID: sec10-F01 | anchor: A01
Your mental and emotional state and your physical health shape how you drive, and poor health, fatigue or feelings such as anger or worry can make you unsafe. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec10-F02 | anchor: A01
If you notice you are just going through the motions without really tracking what is happening around you, stop to rest or end your driving for the day. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec10-F03 | anchor: A01
Drivers under 18 years of age may not use a cell phone or any other mobile electronic device while driving, so turn it off or put it in the back seat. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec10-F04 | anchor: A01
Drivers 18 or older may use a cell phone or other mobile electronic device only with a hands-free accessory that needs no more than minimal finger use to switch on or off. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec10-F05 | anchor: A01
It is illegal to have a TV, tablet or other video display where the driver can see it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec10-F06 | anchor: A01
It is illegal to play a radio or other sound system loud enough to be heard 50 feet from your vehicle, since you need to hear horns, screeching tires and sirens. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec10-F07 | anchor: A01
Anything that takes your eyes off the road while driving is dangerous, such as texting, reading, eating, drinking, putting on makeup or taking off clothing. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec10-F08 | anchor: A01
Never hold a person, a pet or a package in your lap or arms while driving. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec10-F09 | anchor: A01
Do not turn around to tend to passengers, children or pets; if they need attention, pull to the side of the road and park first. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec10-F10 | anchor: A02
Road rage is angry or aggressive behavior by drivers, such as driving in an illegal, unsafe or threatening way, shouting or making rude gestures. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec10-F11 | anchor: A02
If you meet an aggressive driver, stay out of the way and do not challenge them by speeding up or trying to out-drive them. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec10-F12 | anchor: A02
Frequent yawning, head nodding, heavy eyelids, blurred vision and drifting out of your lane are signs you may be falling asleep at the wheel. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec10-F13 | anchor: A02
A tired driver reacts more slowly and notices changing road and traffic conditions less, so be well rested before and during a trip and take breaks when you feel tired. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec10-F14 | anchor: A02
Never keep driving drowsy just to reach your destination; pull over somewhere safe to rest, or get out for a brisk walk. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec10-F15 | anchor: A02
To stay awake, drink water because dehydration causes fatigue, talk with your passenger, and take turns driving so each driver can rest. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec10-F16 | anchor: A02
Be wary of medicines that can make you drowsy. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec10-F17 | anchor: A03
If you are sick, think honestly about whether you are fit to drive, especially for a long trip. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec10-F18 | anchor: A03
Some medical conditions can cause confusion, slower reaction time or a sudden loss of consciousness, so ask your doctor how your condition may affect your driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec10-F19 | anchor: A03
Hearing matters while driving: tire noise changes with the road surface, engine noise can signal a problem, sound can reveal a vehicle in your blind spot, and you need to hear emergency vehicles. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec10-F20 | anchor: A03
Do not wear headphones that could reduce your hearing while driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec10-F21 | anchor: A03
Never drive after drinking alcohol or using other drugs, because they raise your chance of a collision that can cause serious injury or death; let someone else drive. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec10-F22 | anchor: A03
Driving while alcohol or drugs are affecting you can get you arrested for DUII. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec10-F23 | anchor: A03
Oregon law presumes you are impaired at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08% or more, but you can still be arrested with a BAC below 0.08%. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec10-F24 | anchor: A03
Alcohol is the drug most often involved in impaired driving, marijuana impairment has also contributed to many Oregon collisions, and using the two together further reduces your ability to drive. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec10-F25 | anchor: A04
Over-the-counter and prescription medicines can also impair driving, so ask a doctor or pharmacist about side effects, and if you are unsure after starting a new medicine, use other transportation. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec10-F26 | anchor: A04
Oregon's DUII law covers any substance that impairs your mental or physical ability to drive, not just alcohol. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec10-F27 | anchor: A04
Under Oregon's Implied Consent law, driving a motor vehicle means you have agreed to take a breath, blood or urine test when a police officer asks. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec10-F28 | anchor: A04
Refusing an implied consent test can bring a fine, a suspension of your driving privileges, or both. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec10-F29 | anchor: A04
Oregon has a zero tolerance law: a driver under 21 fails the test with a blood alcohol concentration of any amount. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec10-F30 | anchor: A04
A driver aged 21 or over fails the test with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08 percent or more. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec10-F31 | anchor: A04
Oregon's Open Container law makes it illegal to have an open bottle or other container of alcohol in a vehicle on any road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec10-F32 | anchor: A04
A container counts as open once its seal is broken, even if it has been closed again, and any open container belongs in the trunk. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec10-F33 | anchor: A05
No one of any age should ride in a pickup bed or on any outside part of a vehicle. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec10-F34 | anchor: A05
Oregon law forbids anyone under 18 from riding on a hood, fender, running board, pickup bed or other outside part of a vehicle. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec10-F35 | anchor: A05
A dog may ride on an outside part of a vehicle, including a pickup bed, only if a framework, carrier or other device keeps it from falling off. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec10-F36 | anchor: A05
Good maintenance prevents most equipment failures, an unmaintained vehicle can become unsafe, and your owner's manual lists the maintenance it needs. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec10-F37 | anchor: A05
A front tire blowout makes steering hard and can pull the vehicle strongly to one side, while a rear blowout makes the back of the vehicle weave or sway. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec10-F38 | anchor: A05
After a blowout, grip the steering wheel firmly, slow down gradually and pull off the road. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec10-F39 | anchor: A06
If your brakes fail, pump the pedal, which may build enough pressure to get them working again. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec10-F40 | anchor: A06
With failed brakes, shift to a lower gear so the engine helps slow the vehicle, and apply the parking brake slowly. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec10-F41 | anchor: A06
With failed brakes, warn other drivers with your horn or lights that you cannot control the vehicle, and once you have slowed, ease onto the shoulder. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0093]

Misconceptions: an adult may use a phone while driving only through a hands-free accessory, and a driver under eighteen may not use one at all; a BAC under the presumed-impaired level does not protect you from a DUII arrest; DUII covers medicines and marijuana, not just alcohol; a resealed bottle still counts as an open container; slamming the brakes after a blowout is wrong, you slow gradually; a pickup bed is not a legal seat for minors.
Mnemonics: grip, slow, pull off for a blowout; pump, downshift, parking brake, warn, shoulder for failed brakes; under twenty-one means zero; seal broken means open.
Glossary: DUII means driving under the influence of intoxicants; BAC means blood alcohol concentration; implied consent means agreeing, by driving, to a breath, blood or urine test when police ask; zero tolerance means any amount of alcohol fails the test for a driver under twenty-one; hands-free accessory means a device that lets an adult use a phone with minimal finger use.
Dynamic facts: none in these pages; the device, blood alcohol and open container rules are fixed statements of the current manual and can change only with new law.

corpus_stability.reason: The Oregon Driver Manual is a two-year edition (the front cover names a two-year span and the back cover carries a single form revision code); fees and office details are sent to the DMV website rather than printed, and nothing in the selected pages suggests more than one rewrite per year.
